legends: D N VALENTINIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The Pannonian officer who founded the Valentinianic dynasty ruled the West from Trier and Milan, leaving the East to his brother Valens. Their bronze is endlessly repetitive and enormously common: GLORIA ROMANORVM (emperor dragging a captive and holding a labarum) and SECVRITAS REIPVBLICAE (Victory advancing), distinguished by hundreds of mint and field marks, a paradise for specialists at Siscia and Aquileia. Gold shows the emperor holding a labarum and Victory (RESTITVTOR REIPVBLICAE) or two emperors enthroned (VICTORIA AVGG); siliquae show Roma seated (VRBS ROMA). His reform of precious metals c. 367-368 introduced OB and PS marks.
coinage.rarity: Bronze extremely common; gold and siliquae common for the period.
coinage.confusions: Valentinian I, II and III all read D N VALENTINIANVS P F AVG: Valentinian I's bronzes are the GLORIA/SECVRITAS AE3s of 364-375; Valentinian II uses REPARATIO REIPVB AE2s and SALVS REIPVBLICAE AE4s (378-392), sometimes with IVN; Valentinian III (425-455) is mostly gold with D N PLA VALENTINIANVS.
coinage.dating: 364-375; issues by mint field marks and OB/PS marks after c. 367.

legends: D N VALENS P F AVG
coinage.text: Emperor of the East, killed by the Goths at Adrianople in 378. His coins share all the Valentinianic types and were struck at every mint, including western ones, so they are among the most common late Roman coins. The Szilágysomlyó treasure contains his spectacular gold multiples, given to barbarian leaders. Valens's portrait is round-faced with a fleshy neck.
coinage.confusions: The usurper Valens of 316 (Licinius' colleague) is different.

legends: D N PROCOPIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: A relative of Julian who seized Constantinople in September 365 and held it until May 366. His bronzes (REPARATIO FEL TEMP, the emperor holding a labarum and shield, often with a chi-rho in the field) and his bearded portrait in Julian's manner advertised Constantinian legitimacy. Gold is rare. The revolt prompted Valentinian and Valens' tightening of mint controls.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N GRATIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Valentinian I's son, Augustus from the age of eight (367), ruled the West after 375 and was killed in 383 by Magnus Maximus' supporters. Arles struck GLORIA NOVI SAECVLI for his accession; from 378 the large AE2 REPARATIO REIPVB (emperor raising a kneeling woman) was struck for all emperors. His siliquae from Trier are common in British hoards.
coinage.confusions: Shares types with Valentinian II and Theodosius.

legends: D N VALENTINIANVS IVN P F AVG
D N VALENTINIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Proclaimed at four in 375, Valentinian II reigned under the tutelage of his mother Justina, Ambrose and later Arbogast, who probably engineered his death at Vienne in 392. His bronze includes the tiny AE4 SALVS REIPVBLICAE (Victory dragging a captive) and VICTORIA AVGGG. Gold and siliquae are common.
coinage.confusions: IVN in the legend identifies early issues; otherwise see Valentinian I and III.

legends: D N THEODOSIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The last emperor to rule the whole empire. His coinage introduced the tremissis (c. 383) and includes the AE2 VIRTVS EXERCITI and GLORIA ROMANORVM (emperor on a galley or holding a standard), Constantinopolis enthroned (CONCORDIA AVGGG), and the coins of his first wife Aelia Flaccilla (SALVS REIPVBLICAE, Victory inscribing a chi-rho on a shield). From 395 the empire's coinage splits definitively into eastern and western series under Arcadius and Honorius.
coinage.confusions: Theodosius II's coins also read D N THEODOSIVS P F AVG: Theodosius II's gold has a facing helmeted bust and later dates; Theodosius I's bronze is mostly AE2/AE4 of 379-395.

coinage.t: Coinage of Magnus Maximus and Flavius Victor
legends: D N MAG MAXIMVS P F AVG
D N FL VICTOR P F AVG
coinage.text: Proclaimed in Britain in 383, Maximus killed Gratian and ruled Britain, Gaul and Spain from Trier, invading Italy in 387. His London solidi and siliquae marked AVGOB and AVGPS (London renamed Augusta) are among the rarest late Roman coins. Trier siliquae with VIRTVS ROMANORVM (Roma seated) are common in British hoards. His son Flavius Victor, made Augustus as a child, appears on AE4 SPES ROMANORVM (camp gate) and gold. Theodosius defeated and executed both in 388.
coinage.rarity: Trier siliquae common; London issues extremely rare; Victor scarce.
coinage.confusions: Maximus' AVG mark (London) vs AQ (Aquileia).

legends: D N EVGENIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: A grammarian and court official raised by Arbogast after Valentinian II's death, Eugenius is shown bearded, a rare sight in the period and possibly a nod to Julian and pagan intellectual traditions; his regime backed the last pagan revival in Rome under Nicomachus Flavianus. Theodosius defeated him at the Frigidus in 394. Siliquae from Trier and Milan are the commonest pieces.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N ARCADIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Theodosius' elder son, emperor in the East from 395. Constantinople solidi show Constantinopolis enthroned (CONCORDIA AVGG) and, from c. 397, the facing three-quarter helmeted bust with spear and shield that became the eastern model. His wife Eudoxia, enemy of John Chrysostom, is crowned by the hand of God on her coins. Western mints struck gold for him in Honorius' name pairings.
coinage.confusions: Joint issues with Honorius and Theodosius II; check the obverse name.

legends: D N HONORIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Emperor in the West from 395, he moved the court and mint to Ravenna in 402. His standard solidus (VICTORIA AVGGG, emperor holding a standard and Victory, foot on a captive; R-V or M-D in the field) is one of the commonest late Roman gold coins. Siliquae from Milan and Trier dominate the Hoxne hoard. His reign saw Alaric's sack of Rome (410), the loss of Britain and the usurpations of Constantine III, Jovinus and Attalus, all with their own coins.
coinage.rarity: Solidi common; bronze scarcer in the West.
coinage.confusions: Eastern solidi for Honorius from Constantinople (CONOB, three-quarter bust) vs western issues.

coinage.issuerName: Constantine III (with Constans II and Maximus of Spain)
legends: D N CONSTANTINVS P F AVG
D N CONSTANS P F AVG
D N MAXIMVS P F AVG
coinage.text: A soldier proclaimed in Britain in 407 who crossed to Gaul, Constantine III was recognised briefly by Honorius before being besieged at Arles and executed (411). His siliquae and solidi from Trier, Lyon and Arles (VICTORIA AAVGGG, with the doubled A for multiple Augusti) are the latest coins in the Hoxne hoard and so date the end of Roman Britain's coin supply. His son Constans struck rare coins as co-Augustus; his general Gerontius set up Maximus in Spain, whose siliquae from Barcelona are very rare.
coinage.rarity: Siliquae scarce; solidi rare; Constans and Maximus very rare.
coinage.confusions: Constantine III's coins read D N CONSTANTINVS P F AVG like Constantine II's of 337-340: the AAVGGG legend and 5th-century style decide; not to be confused with Constantine III Heraclius (641).

coinage.text: Prefect of Rome made emperor by Alaric in 409 to pressure Honorius, deposed in 410 before the sack, and raised again by Athaulf in Gaul in 414-415. The Rome mint struck fine gold and silver for him with INVICTA ROMA AETERNA, an ironic slogan months before Alaric's sack. Very rare.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N IOVINVS P F AVG
D N SEBASTIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: A Gallo-Roman noble proclaimed at Mainz in 411 with Burgundian and Alan support, Jovinus made his brother Sebastianus co-emperor. Athaulf's Visigoths, acting for Honorius, captured both in 413. His siliquae from Trier and Lyon are the last coins of the Gallic mints for a usurper based in the north.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N THEODOSIVS P F AVG
IMP XXXXII COS XVII P P
coinage.text: Emperor for 48 years, Theodosius II paid huge subsidies to the Huns, whose treasuries are reflected in finds such as the Szikáncs hoard (1,439 of his solidi). His VOT XX MVLT XXX solidus (c. 420-422) shows Victory holding a long jewelled cross, the first time the cross dominates a Roman gold coin; the IMP XXXXII COS XVII P P type (Constantinopolis seated, 441-443) records his titles explicitly. His AE4 are tiny, often with a cross in a wreath. His sister Pulcheria and wife Eudocia have abundant coins.
keyTypes: VOT XX MVLT XXX long cross
coinage.confusions: Theodosius I (see above).
coinage.dating: VOT and IMP/COS numbers date solidi closely.

legends: D N CONSTANTIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Honorius' great general, husband of Galla Placidia and father of Valentinian III, co-Augustus for seven months in 421, never recognised in the East. His Ravenna solidi are very rare.
coinage.confusions: Constantius II (4th century, diademed).

legends: D N IOHANNES P F AVG
coinage.text: The primicerius notariorum proclaimed at Rome after Honorius' death in 423, supported by Aetius, who went to recruit Huns for him. An eastern army installed the child Valentinian III and executed Joannes at Aquileia in 425. His coins, unusually, show him bearded.
coinage.confusions: None.

coinage.issuerName: Valentinian III (with Galla Placidia, Licinia Eudoxia and Honoria)
legends: D N PLA VALENTINIANVS P F AVG
D N GALLA PLACIDIA P F AVG
IVST GRAT HONORIA P F AVG
coinage.text: The commonest western gold of the 5th century: VICTORIA AVGGG with the emperor holding a long cross and Victory on a globe, his foot on a human-headed serpent, struck at Ravenna, Rome and Milan. His mother Galla Placidia (regent 425-437), his sister Honoria (who appealed to Attila) and his wife Licinia Eudoxia all have coins. Western bronze becomes scarce and crude. His murder in 455, avenging Aetius, opened the final collapse of the western dynasty.
coinage.rarity: Solidi common; Honoria rare; Licinia Eudoxia scarce.
coinage.confusions: PLA (Placidius) distinguishes him from Valentinian I and II.
coinage.dating: 425-455; mint marks RV, RM, MD, AR in field.

legends: D N MARCIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The officer chosen as husband for Pulcheria in 450, Marcian stopped tribute to Attila and called the Council of Chalcedon (451). His Constantinople solidi (VICTORIA AVGGG, Victory with long cross) are common; AE4 nummi carry his monogram. Western mints struck gold for him under Valentinian III.
coinage.confusions: Officina numerals on solidi identify sub-issues.

legends: D N PETRONIVS MAXIMVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The senator who succeeded Valentinian III in March 455 and was killed by a mob in May as Gaiseric's Vandals approached Rome. His solidi are rare and highly prized.
coinage.confusions: Magnus Maximus (4th century).

legends: D N AVITVS PERP F AVG
coinage.text: A Gallo-Roman aristocrat proclaimed at Arles with Visigothic backing (his son-in-law was Sidonius Apollinaris, who wrote his panegyric). His Arles solidi, with A-R in the field, are among the few Gallic gold issues of the period. Ricimer and Majorian deposed him in 456.
coinage.confusions: None.

coinage.text: Leo's Constantinople solidi (facing helmeted bust; Victory with long cross) are abundant and found widely in Scandinavia. His tiny AE4s include a lion reverse, a pun on his name, as well as monograms. His wife Verina and the western emperors he sponsored (Anthemius, Julius Nepos) appear in parallel. He financed the disastrous expedition against the Vandals (468).
coinage.confusions: Leo II (474) with Zeno.

legends: D N IVLIVS MAIORIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The last effective western emperor, Majorian campaigned in Gaul and Spain and prepared a fleet against the Vandals that was destroyed at Cartagena (460). Ricimer had him killed in 461. His solidi, with the emperor holding cross and globe over a human-headed serpent, are rarer than Valentinian III's.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N LIBIVS SEVERVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Ricimer's puppet, never recognised by Leo I. His solidi are the latest coins in the Patching hoard from Sussex, showing that western gold still reached Britain in the 460s.
coinage.confusions: None.

coinage.text: An eastern aristocrat sent by Leo I to rule the West. His solidi show two emperors (Anthemius and Leo) standing and holding a cross on a globe between them, SALVS REIPVBLICAE: a statement of East-West partnership. His wife Euphemia, Marcian's daughter, has rare coins. Ricimer besieged and killed him in Rome in 472.
coinage.confusions: Anthemius of Tralles is the architect of Hagia Sophia.

coinage.text: Ricimer's last emperor, husband of Valentinian III's daughter Placidia, reigned from April to November 472. His solidi carry a simple cross with SALVS MVNDI ('salvation of the world'), the first Roman coin with the cross alone as the reverse type and the legend proclaiming Christ's salvation, a striking break with the Victory types.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N GLYCERIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The comes domesticorum raised by the Burgundian Gundobad in 473 and deposed by Julius Nepos in 474, after which he became bishop of Salona. Rare solidi and tremisses.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N IVL NEPOS P F AVG
coinage.text: Nephew of Marcellinus of Dalmatia, installed by Leo I in 474 and driven out by Orestes in 475. Recognised in the East as western emperor until his death in Dalmatia in 480, he continued to be named on coins struck in Italy and Gaul after 476, including issues of Odoacer, which makes him, technically, the last legitimate western emperor.
coinage.confusions: Posthumous-style issues of Odoacer in his name.

legends: D N LEO ET ZENO PP AVG
coinage.text: Leo I's grandson, son of Zeno and Ariadne, became emperor as a child in January 474, crowned his father Zeno co-emperor in February and died in November. Joint solidi name both.
coinage.confusions: Leo I (D N LEO PERPET AVG).

coinage.text: The Isaurian general who married Leo I's daughter Ariadne. His reign was interrupted by Basiliscus (475-476). In the West Odoacer struck gold in Zeno's name at Milan, Ravenna and Rome after 476, so western 'Zeno' solidi are a principal source for Odoacer's Italy. Eastern solidi are common.
coinage.confusions: Separate first and second reigns by officina marks and style.

legends: D N BASILISCI ET MARC P AVG
coinage.text: Verina's brother, commander of the failed Vandal expedition of 468, seized Constantinople in 475 and was overthrown by Zeno in 476. Joint coins with his son Marcus and coins of his wife Zenonis are rare. His anti-Chalcedonian 'Encyclical' alienated the capital.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N ROMVLVS AVGVSTVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Son of Orestes, set up as emperor in October 475 at about 14 and deposed by Odoacer in September 476, an event later treated as the 'fall of the Western Empire'. His coins are standard late western types, and their symbolic value has made them expensive and widely forged.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: D N IVL NEPOS P F AVG
coinage.text: Odoacer did not call himself emperor and struck gold only in the names of Julius Nepos and Zeno. His own name and moustached portrait appear on rare silver from Ravenna (FL ODOVAC), the first portrait of a barbarian king of Italy on a coin. At Rome large bronzes revived the old image of the city (INVICTA ROMA, she-wolf), probably under senatorial control. His coins are scarce and important for the transition from Roman to Ostrogothic Italy.
coinage.rarity: Own-name coins very rare; imperial-name solidi scarce.
coinage.confusions: Separating Odoacer-period western solidi from late imperial ones requires specialist catalogues.

legends: D N ANASTASIVS P F AVG
D N IVSTINVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Theodoric struck gold in the names of Anastasius and Justin I, with silver bearing his monogram on the reverse, maintaining the fiction of subordination to Constantinople while ruling Italy. The one exception is the Senigallia medallion, a triple solidus showing Theodoric with moustache and long hair, holding a Victory on a globe, with REX THEODERICVS PIVS PRINCIS and VICTOR GENTIVM, found in 1894 at Morro d'Alba near Senigallia (Museo Nazionale Romano): the only certain portrait of him. Rome's senatorial bronzes continued.
coinage.rarity: Monogram silver scarce; gold in imperial names scarce; medallion unique.
coinage.confusions: Eastern vs Ostrogothic solidi in Anastasius' name: style, officina marks and letters.

coinage.text: Anastasius' great bronze reform (498, revised c. 512) created the follis with its large M and the system of 40, 20, 10 and 5 nummi that Byzantine coinage kept for centuries. His solidi continue the facing helmeted bust and Victory with long cross. He left a treasury surplus of 320,000 pounds of gold according to Procopius (Secret History 19.7). Western barbarian kings imitated his solidi widely.
coinage.confusions: Anastasius II (713-715) is an 8th-century emperor with very different coins; Ostrogothic solidi in his name.
coinage.dating: Light folles 498-c. 512; heavy folles after c. 512.

legends: D N IVSTIN ET IVSTINIAN PP AVG
coinage.text: The illiterate peasant-soldier from Bederiana who rose to the throne. His solidi replace Victory with a facing angel holding a long cross and a globus cruciger. In April-August 527 he and his nephew Justinian appear seated together on joint solidi and folles. Antioch's folles mark the earthquake years; Thessalonica struck its special 16-nummi pieces.
coinage.confusions: Justin II (565-578): Justin II's folles show him enthroned with Sophia, and his solidi have Constantinopolis seated.

coinage.text: Justinian's coinage follows the reconquests: new mints at Carthage (533), Ravenna and Rome (540s-550s). Early solidi have the three-quarter helmeted bust; from the late 530s-540s he appears facing, helmeted with plumes and holding a globus cruciger. From his 12th regnal year (538/9) folles are dated (ANNO with the year) and enlarged to about 22-25 g, then reduced from c. 542 in the aftermath of the plague. The 36-solidus gold medallion showing him on horseback (once in the Cabinet des Médailles, stolen and melted in 1831) is known from electrotypes. His folles are among the most collected Byzantine coins.
coinage.confusions: Joint issues of 527 with Justin I; Justinian II (685-711) is a different emperor.
coinage.dating: Regnal year on folles from 538/9 (year 12) to 565 (year 38).

coinage.text: Justinian's nephew is best known numismatically for the folles showing him and his formidable wife Sophia seated side by side on a double throne, haloed: the first regular coins depicting an empress beside the emperor as a co-ruler. His solidi show Constantinopolis seated, helmeted, holding a globe and spear. His mental collapse in 574 led to the regency of Tiberius.
coinage.confusions: Justin I (profile or three-quarter busts; angel solidus).

legends: D N TIb CONSTANT PP AVG
coinage.text: Tiberius introduced the cross on four steps on the solidus reverse, the dominant Byzantine gold type for a century, and folles with the emperor in consular robes holding a mappa and eagle-tipped sceptre. Known for open-handed generosity, he was remembered in the West through Gregory of Tours' anecdotes about treasure found under a palace slab.
coinage.confusions: Tiberius III (698-705) has later coins with different style.

legends: D N MAVRC TIb PP AVG
D N mAVRIC TIbER PP AVG
coinage.text: Maurice's long reign produced an abundant coinage across the network, including the new Sicilian mint at Catania and the remarkable Cherson bronzes showing Maurice with his empress Constantina and their son Theodosius. His solidi show an angel with a staff topped by a christogram and a globus cruciger. Carthage's issues for him are small and thick. His fiscal stringency with the army led to the mutiny of 602 and his murder by Phocas.
coinage.confusions: Legend abbreviations vary greatly by mint.

coinage.text: The centurion who murdered Maurice is the first legitimate emperor since Julian shown bearded on the coinage (usurpers such as Procopius, Eugenius and Joannes aside), wearing a crown with a cross, which made his coins stand out from his predecessors'. Folles show him and his wife Leontia standing together. His coins were heavily overstruck by Heraclius, and finds of overstrikes are evidence for the damnatio of his memory and the shortage of metal during the Persian war that his reign provoked.
coinage.confusions: Heraclian overstrikes on Phocas folles.

legends: DD NN HERACLIVS ET HERA CONST PP AVG
coinage.text: Heraclius' gold sequence is a family album that dates itself: consular busts of the two Heraclii during the revolt (608-610); Heraclius alone with short beard (610-613); Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine facing (613-c. 629), the father's beard growing longer and the son's appearing; and from c. 632 three standing figures (Heraclius, Heraclius Constantine, Heraclonas). The silver hexagram (615) with DEVS ADIVTA ROMANIS was struck from melted church plate. Folles are light, often overstruck on Phocas', and come from emergency mints in Isauria and Cyprus as well as the regular network. The officina letter after VICTORIA AVGU (Greek numerals A-I) and the CONOB mark identify Constantinople gold.
coinage.rarity: Solidi very common; hexagrams common; revolt issues rare.
coinage.confusions: Distinguish Heraclian solidi from those of Constans II (641-668), which continue the three-figure and facing types; Carthage 'globular' solidi are a separate series.
coinage.dating: Beard lengths and the number of figures date solidi; folles carry regnal years (often illegible).

legends: DD NN HERACLIVS ET HERA CONST PP AVG
coinage.text: Crowned co-emperor as an infant in 613, Heraclius Constantine appears on almost all of his father's coins, ageing from a small child to a bearded young man. He reigned alone from February to May 641 before dying of tuberculosis (rumour blamed his stepmother Martina). Coins struck specifically for his sole reign have been proposed but are disputed; for collectors he is a constant presence on Heraclian coins rather than an issuer in his own right.
coinage.rarity: Common as co-ruler; any sole-reign attribution is doubtful.
coinage.confusions: Constantine III the usurper of 407-411 is a different person.

legends: (no legend naming him on most coins)
coinage.text: Son of Heraclius and Martina, Heraclonas appears as the third standing figure on his father's solidi from c. 632 and was made Augustus in 638. After his half-brother's death in 641 he reigned briefly with Martina before the Senate and army deposed them, cutting his nose and her tongue, in favour of Constans II. Solidi attributed to his short sole reign (with figures of Heraclonas and a junior) remain controversial.
coinage.rarity: As co-ruler common; sole-reign coins disputed.
coinage.confusions: Early Constans II solidi.
